facts.statement: In 2024, 563 million people in sub-Saharan Africa had no electricity, 86 per cent of the world's total.
facts.source_org: UN Statistics Division (SDG Extended Report 2026, storyline from Tracking SDG7 custodians)
facts.quote: Sub Saharan Africa has become the center of the global challenge, accounting for 563 million—or 86 percent—of people without electricity worldwide.
facts.notes: Verified in retrieved PDF (inputs as of 30 April 2026). Do not mix with SEforALL's whole-Africa figure (581 million, 88.8%), which covers a different geography.

facts.statement: In 2024, 655 million people worldwide still had no electricity, only 11.5 million fewer than in 2023.
facts.source_org: UN Statistics Division (SDG Extended Report 2026, Goal 7)
facts.quote: In 2024, the global access rate remained at 92 percent, leaving 655 million people without electricity—only 11.5 million fewer than in 2023.
facts.notes: The quoted sentence appears word for word. SEforALL rounds the fall to 'about 11 million fewer'.

facts.statement: In 2024, Nigeria had the largest population without electricity of any country, about 87 million people.
facts.source_org: Sustainable Energy for All, analysis of Tracking SDG7 2026 datasets (IEA, IRENA, UNSD, World Bank, WHO)
facts.quote: Nigeria has the largest unelectrified population, followed by DR Congo and Ethiopia. [Chart 'Population without electricity access, millions, 2024': labels 87, 85, 57, 33, 22 ...]
facts.notes: The ranking is stated in the text. The figure 87 is the largest bar label on the chart, so it belongs to Nigeria, but text extraction cannot pair bars with names directly. Print it as 'about 87 million'. The UN Extended Report backs the top-three ranking: 'Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Ethiopia alone representing nearly one third of the total'.

facts.statement: In 2024, about 997 million people in Africa had no clean cooking, more than the 911 million in Asia, and Africa is the only region where that number is still rising.
facts.source_org: Sustainable Energy for All, analysis of Tracking SDG7 2026 datasets
facts.quote: Africa is the largest deficit region, and the only one still rising. » Africa’s deficit (~997M) has overtaken Asia’s (~911M) - the centre of gravity has shifted to Sub-Saharan Africa.
facts.notes: Page 14 adds: 'its absolute deficit (approximately 997 million in 2024) has now overtaken Asia’s (approximately 911 million)'. The report warns that these deficits are summed from country data and come out slightly below the headline totals.

facts.statement: Nearly two billion people still cook with wood, charcoal and other polluting fuels, half of them in Africa, and in 2024 only 23 per cent of people in sub-Saharan Africa had access to clean cooking.
facts.value: nearly 2 billion globally; half in Africa; 23% access in sub-Saharan Africa (2024)
facts.source_org: International Energy Agency
facts.quote: Nearly two billion people still cook using wood, charcoal and other fuels that produce harmful smoke ... half of the two billion people still lacking access globally live in Africa. ... As of 2024, 23% of sub-Saharan Africans have access to clean cooking, an increase of almost 1 percentage point from the previous year.
facts.notes: Every part of the claim appears on the retrieved page. Credit the 23% to the IEA, because the WHO figure in the UN Extended Report is 22% (range 20–25%) for sub-Saharan Africa in 2024.

facts.statement: In 2025 Africa accounted for only 2 per cent of global clean energy investment despite having 20 per cent of the world's population (IEA estimate).
facts.value: 2% of clean energy investment vs 20% of world population
facts.source_org: International Energy Agency
facts.quote: Africa accounts for only 2% of clean energy investment despite having 20% of the world population.
facts.notes: World Energy Investment 2025, Executive summary. The same page notes that 2025 values are estimated.

facts.statement: Energy investment in Africa in 2025 is one-third lower than in 2015, and debt servicing costs equal more than 85 per cent of the continent's total energy investment in 2025 (IEA estimate).
facts.value: -33% since 2015; debt service over 85% of energy investment
facts.source_org: International Energy Agency
facts.quote: in Africa, overall debt servicing costs are equivalent to over 85% of total energy investment in 2025. Energy investments in Africa are one-third lower in 2025 than they were in 2015, as a decline in oil and gas spending has been only partially offset by higher investments in renewable power.
facts.notes: The quote matches the source word for word. 2025 values are estimated.

facts.statement: Africa is home to 60 per cent of the world's best solar resources (IEA, Africa Energy Outlook 2022).
facts.source_org: International Energy Agency
facts.quote: Africa is home to 60% of the best solar resources globally, yet only 1% of installed solar PV capacity.
facts.notes: Confirmed on the AEO 2022 key findings page. The '1% of installed PV' part of that sentence is from 2022. For the current installed share, use the IRENA 2025 figure (0.88%).

facts.statement: At the end of 2025 Africa had 21,003 MW of installed solar PV capacity, less than 1 per cent (0.88 per cent) of the world total of 2,383,162 MW (IRENA).
facts.source_org: IRENA
facts.notes: Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026, PDF page 37, solar PV table. The 0.88% share is our own calculation (21003/2383162 = 0.881%). IRENA does not state that percentage.

facts.statement: In the first quarter of 2026 Nigeria's 28 grid-connected power plants had 13,625 MW of installed capacity but averaged only 4,457.96 MW available, a plant availability factor of 32.72 per cent (NERC).
facts.source_org: Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC)
facts.quote: In 2026/Q1, the average plant availability factor for all grid-connected plants was 32.72%, meaning that 67.28% of the total installed capacity across the twenty-eight (28) grid-connected power plants was unavailable for dispatch at any given time during the quarter. [Table 1: Total 13,625 5,400.38 4,457.96 39.64 32.72]
facts.notes: The Table 1 total row is on report page 17 (PDF page 23). The report leaves out AES and Gbarain because they are not operational. Average available capacity fell 942.42 MW (-17.45%) from 5,400.38 MW in 2025 Q4. Notes are in scratchpad/research/fc-africa-nerc-x7/notes.md.

facts.statement: In the first quarter of 2026 Nigeria's grid generated an average of 4,112.72 MWh per hour (8,883.47 GWh in total), against 13,625 MW of installed capacity across its 28 grid-connected power plants.
facts.value: 4,112.72 MWh/h average hourly generation; 13,625 MW installed (28 plants)
facts.source_org: Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC)
facts.quote: The average hourly generation on the grid in 2026/Q1 was 4,112.72MWh/h, which translates to a total generation of 8,883.47GWh.
facts.notes: Quote on p.3 and p.18 of the 94-page PDF. 13,625 MW is the 'Total' installed-capacity row of Table 1 (p.17), which covers the 28 grid-connected plants, not all capacity in Nigeria. Same report: average plant availability factor 32.72%, so 67.28% of installed capacity was unavailable; Q1 output was down 7.64% from 4,452.71 MWh/h in 2025 Q4. Notes: research/factcheck-nigeria-energy-2026-10-02.md

facts.statement: About 86 per cent of businesses in Nigeria own or share a generator, and Nigeria has the world's largest market for private backup petrol and diesel generators (IFC, 2025).
facts.source_org: IFC / World Bank Group
facts.quote: About 86 percent of businesses in Nigeria own or share a generator. This situation has led to Nigeria having the world’s largest market for private backup gasoline and diesel generators.
facts.notes: Nigeria Country Private Sector Diagnostic, May 2025, PDF page 24. The wording matches word for word.

facts.statement: More than 65 per cent of Nigeria's installed generation is unavailable because of poor maintenance, vandalism or ageing, and the lack of reliable electricity costs an estimated 5 to 7 per cent of GDP a year (IFC, 2025).
facts.source_org: IFC / World Bank Group
facts.quote: More than 65 percent of installed generation is unavailable because of poor maintenance, vandalism or aging, forcing millions of homes and businesses to keep diesel generators on hand. Economic losses from the lack of reliable electricity are estimated at 5 to 7 percent of GDP annually.
facts.notes: Executive Summary, p.ix (PDF page 11), May 2025. NERC's Q1 2026 report agrees with it (67.28% of installed capacity unavailable).

facts.statement: Nigeria was one of nine countries that together accounted for 83 per cent of global gas flaring in 2025 while producing 46 per cent of the world's oil, and ranked eighth among them by flare volume (World Bank, 2026).
facts.value: 8th by 2025 flare volume; top nine = 83% of global flaring
facts.source_org: World Bank, Global Flaring and Methane Reduction Partnership
facts.quote: Nine countries (Russia, Iran, Iraq, Venezuela, Mexico, Libya, Algeria, Nigeria, and the United States) accounted for 83 percent of global flare volumes in 2025 while producing only 46 percent of the world's oil. [footnote xviii: This order represents the volume in 2025.]
facts.notes: Global Gas Flaring Tracker Report, June 2026. Figure 13, 'Flare volumes in the top 30 flaring countries, 2021-2025 (in order of 2025 flare volume)', lists Nigeria eighth. The report also says Nigeria's flaring volumes and oil production each rose 8 per cent in 2025.

facts.statement: In 2025 Nigeria's gas flaring volumes and its oil production both rose by 8 per cent.
facts.source_org: World Bank, Global Flaring and Methane Reduction Partnership (Global Gas Flaring Tracker Report, June 2026)
facts.quote: Nigeria also saw flaring volumes and oil production rise by 8 percent. Insufficient infrastructure to bring the associated gas to markets and aging gas processing plants with high downtime rates contribute to Nigeria’s high flaring levels.
facts.notes: Found in the country section of the June 2026 report. Notes: scratchpad/research/fc-nigeria/notes.md

facts.statement: Global gas flaring rose from 157 billion cubic metres in 2024 to 167 billion cubic metres in 2025, up 6 per cent, the highest level since 2019 and the third consecutive annual increase.
facts.source_org: World Bank, Global Flaring and Methane Reduction Partnership (Global Gas Flaring Tracker Report, June 2026)
facts.quote: Global gas flaring increased from 157 bcm in 2024 to 167 bcm in 2025, a 6 percent increase, the highest level since 2019 and the third consecutive annual increase, while oil production grew by only 3.3 percent, meaning flaring rose at a faster rate than output.
facts.notes: Key Findings, item 1.

facts.statement: The Dangote refinery's original nameplate capacity was 650,000 barrels per day, and in early 2026 its managing director, David Bird, said 'This is the year we sustain full nameplate capacity'. The U.S. EIA reports that maintenance finished in February 2026 raised capacity to 700,000 barrels per day.
facts.value: 650,000 bpd nameplate (insured); 700,000 b/d after February 2026 maintenance per EIA
facts.source_org: Hydrocarbon Processing (trade press, 4 Feb 2026); superseded on capacity by U.S. EIA Today in Energy, 24 Aug 2026
facts.quote: Nigeria's Dangote Refinery will begin performance test runs at its full nameplate capacity of 650,000 bpd in February after completing planned maintenance, a senior executive said on Wednesday ... "This is the year we sustain full nameplate capacity." ... Bird said the plant is insured at 650,000 bpd but has enough design margin to increase capacity to 700,000 bpd
facts.notes: The quote supports 650k and the Bird statement. The article says 'said on Wednesday' and gives the tests as coming 'in February', so it does not pin the remark to February; say 'early 2026'. The 650k figure is superseded: EIA (https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=68004) says February 2026 maintenance raised CDU capacity to 700,000 b/d. Do not print 650k as the current capacity.

facts.statement: Maintenance completed in February 2026 raised the Dangote refinery's crude distillation capacity from 650,000 to 700,000 barrels per day, and the Dangote Group plans to add a second 750,000-barrel-per-day distillation unit by 2028.
facts.value: 700,000 b/d; second 750,000 b/d unit planned by 2028
facts.source_org: U.S. Energy Information Administration (Today in Energy, 24 August 2026)
facts.quote: Maintenance completed on the Dangote refinery in February 2026 increased the facility’s crude oil distillation capacity from 650,000 b/d to 700,000 b/d . [...] The Dangote Group plans to double its refinery capacity by adding a second 750,000-b/d crude oil distillation unit by 2028.
facts.notes: The 2028 unit is a company plan as reported by EIA, not a completed fact. The page is dated August 24, 2026.

facts.statement: After the Dangote refinery opened in January 2024, Nigeria's seaborne petroleum product shipments averaged 561,000 barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, against 79,000 barrels per day in 2023. Exports alone rose from 46,000 to 350,000 barrels per day, about seven-fold.
facts.value: Shipments 561,000 b/d in 2Q26 vs 79,000 b/d in 2023; exports 350,000 b/d in 2Q26 vs 46,000 b/d in 2023
facts.source_org: U.S. Energy Information Administration (data: Vortexa Analytics), 24 August 2026
facts.quote: Underpinned by the opening of the Dangote refinery in January 2024, seaborne petroleum product shipments from Nigeria averaged 561,000 barrels per day (b/d) in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), compared with an annual average of 79,000 b/d in 2023, according to data from Vortexa. Of those shipments, 350,000 b/d were exported in 2Q26, compared with an annual average of 46,000 b/d in 2023.
facts.notes: The original claim paired 'exports grew seven-fold' with the 561k figure, but 561k is total shipments, which includes intra-Nigerian coastal shipments of 211k b/d. Exports were 350k b/d. EIA's own lead sentence says 'Seaborne petroleum product exports from Nigeria have grown seven-fold since 2023'.

facts.statement: Nigeria's Energy Transition Plan targets net zero by 2060; its November 2024 update estimates that this needs about USD 500 billion of capital investment above business as usual, which would bring about USD 686 billion in fuel savings (the original 2022 costing put the extra cost at about USD 410 billion).
facts.value: Net zero 2060; about USD 500 billion above business as usual; USD 686 billion fuel savings (original 2022 costing: about USD 410 billion above BAU)
facts.source_org: Nigeria Energy Transition Plan (ETIP update), hosted by Sustainable Energy for All
facts.quote: The updated ETP estimates that achieving net-zero by 2060 would require a capital investment of approximately $500 billion USD above business-as-usual (BAU) levels. However, this investment would result in fuel savings of $686 billion USD, demonstrating significant economic and environmental benefits.
facts.notes: Cover reads 'November 2024 / Nigeria Energy Transition & Investment Plan Update (2024)'; quote on p3. The USD 1.9 trillion total in the input value belongs to the original 2022 costing (p6), not to the update, so do not print it next to the USD 500 billion as if it were the update's total. Notes: scratchpad/research/fc5/factcheck-notes.md

facts.statement: The original 2022 costing of Nigeria's Energy Transition Plan put the net-zero pathway at about USD 1.9 trillion of spending to 2060, including about USD 410 billion above business as usual, or about USD 10 billion a year.
facts.value: ~USD 1.9 trillion total; ~USD 410 billion above BAU; ~USD 10 billion a year
facts.source_org: Nigeria Energy Transition Plan (ETIP update), hosted by Sustainable Energy for All
facts.quote: The initial costing of the ETP indicated that enabling Nigeria’s Net Zero pathway would require ~$1.9 trillion spending up to 2060, including ~$410 billion above business-as-usual spending which translates to about $10 billion per annum.
facts.notes: p6 of the November 2024 update; p5 says 'In 2022, the ETP was developed as a strategy...'. The 2024 update replaces these figures (about USD 500 billion above BAU), so label them as the original 2022 figures.

facts.statement: Nigeria's updated Energy Transition Plan (2024) calls for 277 GW of installed power capacity by 2060, with electricity generation rising 6.5 times between 2020 and 2060.
facts.value: 277 GW by 2060 (ETP 1.0: 274 GW); generation x6.5 (2020 to 2060)
facts.source_org: Nigeria Energy Transition Plan (ETIP update), hosted by Sustainable Energy for All
facts.quote: The updated Energy Transition Plan (ETP 2.0) outlines the need for a total installed power capacity of 277 GW by 2060, similar to the 274 GW projected in the initial ETP 1.0. [...] Electricity generation increases by 6.5 times between 2020-2060, with an annual growth rate of 32% due to universal electrification in 2030
facts.notes: 277 GW is on p3 of the executive summary. The 6.5 times figure is on the p18 power-generation slide of the same update deck. That slide does not itself say ETP 2.0, so this is a minor caveat. The p17 slide also says installed capacity rises 6.8 times between 2020 and 2060.

facts.statement: The IEA expects global energy investment to reach USD 3.4 trillion in 2026, with clean energy investment of USD 2.2 trillion, almost double that going to fossil fuels.
facts.value: USD 3.4 trillion total; USD 2.2 trillion clean; clean almost double fossil
facts.source_org: International Energy Agency
facts.quote: Despite the destabilising effect of the Middle East conflict, capital flows to the energy sector are expected to grow to USD 3.4 trillion in 2026, a 5% rise from 2025, mainly from China, the US, and the EU. Clean energy investment grows to USD 2.2 trillion, almost double that of fossil fuels.
facts.notes: The quote matches the text on the retrieved page word for word (page title 'Regional dashboards – World Energy Investment 2026'). These are expected figures for 2026, so describe them as expected or projected.

facts.statement: According to IRENA, the global weighted-average cost of electricity from new solar PV has fallen 89 per cent since 2010 and stood at USD 44 per megawatt hour in 2025, unchanged from 2024.
facts.source_org: IRENA
facts.quote: Solar photovoltaic (PV) remained at its 2024 level of USD 44 per megawatt hour (MWh). [...] Since 2010, the cost of solar PV has fallen by 89%, onshore wind by 71%, and offshore wind by 63%.
facts.notes: Highlights, p3. The executive summary says 'global, weighted-average levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) for solar PV remained unchanged compared to 2024, at USD 44 per megawatt hour', with footnote 3: 'All values in 2025 USD.' The report covers newly commissioned projects.

facts.statement: The world added a record 692 GW of renewable power capacity in 2025, and Africa recorded its largest increase, adding 11.3 GW to grow its renewable capacity by 15.9 per cent.
facts.source_org: IRENA
facts.quote: 2025 saw total renewable power capacity reach 5149 gigawatts (GW) after the addition of 692 GW ... Africa recorded its highest capacity increase, rising by 15.9% or adding 11.3 GW, driven by Ethiopia, South Africa, and Egypt.
facts.notes: Retrieved 2 Oct 2026. The release also says '2025 marks another record for installed global capacity'. The 15.9% is growth in Africa's installed capacity, not growth in annual additions. Notes: research/fc4/notes.md

facts.statement: In 2025 the global surface air temperature was 1.47°C above the pre-industrial (1850–1900) level, making it the third-warmest year on record, after 1.60°C in 2024, the warmest year.
facts.source_org: Copernicus Climate Change Service (ECMWF)
facts.quote: In 2025, according to ERA5, the global surface air temperature was 1.47°C above the pre-industrial level, following 1.60°C in 2024, the warmest year on record.
facts.notes: Verbatim match; ERA5 dataset, 1850-1900 baseline.

facts.statement: Global energy-related CO2 emissions rose by around 0.4 per cent in 2025 to a new high of nearly 38.4 billion tonnes, 5 per cent above 2019 levels.
facts.source_org: International Energy Agency
facts.quote: Global growth in energy-related CO2 emissions slowed in 2025, rising by around 0.4%, the slowest rate since 2021. Despite this slowdown, total energy-related CO2 emissions increased by around 145 million tonnes (Mt) in 2025, reaching a new high of nearly 38.4 billion tonnes (Gt) 1 , and 5% above 2019 levels.
facts.notes: Verbatim match.

facts.statement: The United Nations projects (2024) that sub-Saharan Africa's population will grow by 79 per cent over the next 30 years, reaching 2.2 billion in 2054.
facts.source_org: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division
facts.quote: Over the next 30 years, the total population of those located in sub- Saharan Africa is projected to see an increase of 79 per cent, reaching 2.2 billion in 2054 (ranging from 2.1 billion to 2.4 billion, with a probability of 95 per cent)
facts.notes: Printed page 36 (PDF page 50). Another '79 per cent' figure on p.12 refers to population momentum's share of global growth; do not conflate.
